newsitem.title: USA: ABC launches irreverent promo campaign.
newsitem.headline: ABC launches irreverent promo campaign.

text.p: The ABC television network unveiled a new promotional campaign Tuesday using slogans such as: The whales can save themselves. Watch TV.
Another is: Books are overrated. Watch TV.

At its annual meeting with local-station affiliates, the network introduced the irreverent promotional spots, which will begin airing this month and escalate as the network gets closer to launching its fall schedule, network officials said.

Robert A. Iger, president of ABC, Inc., promised the No. 3 network will revamp its morning show, "Good Morning America" -- replacing long-time co-host Joan Lunden -- without the kind of mistakes its competitors have suffered in the past.
"We intend to make changes, but we do not intend to make mistakes," Iger said.

He said the past year, which saw ABC struggle to halt its slide from its long-held position atop the network Neilson ratings, has "probably been the most challenging year in my 23 years at the company."

The new president of the ABC Television Network, Preston Padden, just three months into the job, spoke of taking a cue from Steven Spielberg and "digitizing our dinosaurs" -- a reference to broadcast television stations. The network has an aggressive five-year plan to convert them to digital signals.
It was that conversion, more than the network's recent fall in ratings, that seemed to worry station managers.
"Most people feel the network bottomed out a year ago. And who's going to bet against (ABC owner) Disney?" said Steven South, general manager of KAKE in Wichita, Kansas.
"But the digital conversion is going to cost every station millions -- from cameras to towers -- and we're not going to see a dollar of return on it. You either do it, or you lose viewers."

Network officials announced Tuesday that they would help absorb some of that expense by reimbursing affiliates for the cost of receiving equipment the stations must install before they can pick up the new digitized network signals.
Spokeswoman Ann Marie Riccitelli said the network would not release the estimated cost.

The new promotional campaign, which includes a spot assuring parents that their kids are not having unprotected sex or getting tattoos while glued to the TV screen, is the work of TWBA Chiat/Day, the firm which produced memorable campaigns for Nissan and Energizer, said Jim Vescera, the network's senior vice president of Advertising and Promotions.
Vescera said ABC was trying to break away from network slogans such as Must See TV and promotions with big stars posed with big logos because the public no longer can keep them all straight.
"We were looking for advertising that entertains," Vescera said.
Rusty Kirkland, general manager of KESQ in Palm Springs, Calif., said it took a while for him to get used to the new promotions.
"The one I was really worried about was the one that said books are overrated. I just said huh? But after a while, I finally got it."
